analysis.one_liner: Bans advertising targeted to individuals' personal data, allowing only contextual ads.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with one cosponsor, it sat in a House subcommittee from September 2023 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit companies from deciding who sees an ad based on personal information collected about them — their browsing history, location, devices, or profiles. Ads could still run next to content a person is already viewing (contextual advertising), and geographic targeting to a state, city, or media market would stay allowed. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals in court would all be able to enforce the ban, with damages available to individuals and pre-dispute arbitration agreements made unenforceable for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet or connected devices gains a limit on how much of their personal information can be harvested and used to target them with ads. Small advertisers would compete on a more level field against companies with vast data troves.

how_it_helps.text: Bars advertisers and ad intermediaries from targeting ads using personal information — including browsing history, contact details, unique device identifiers, and inferred data [S2].

Keeps contextual advertising (ads placed next to what a person is already viewing or searched for) legal, and permits targeting by recognized place such as a state, city, or media market, so local businesses can still reach local audiences [S2].
Gives the FTC enforcement power — including over common carriers and nonprofits — and lets state attorneys general sue on residents' behalf [S2].

Creates a private right of action with damages of $100–$1,000 per negligent violation and $500–$5,000 per willful violation, plus attorney's fees, and voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims [S2].
Treats a violation involving a person's personal information as a concrete injury, making it easier to get into court [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Online platforms, ad-tech intermediaries, and data brokers that profit from tracking people and selling targeted ad placement lose their core business model, and large advertisers lose the precision targeting they currently buy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ad-tech firms, data brokers, big platforms

drawbacks.text: A blanket ban rather than an opt-out system would also take targeted ads away from small businesses, which use them to reach customers cheaply; they would compete against firms that can afford mass contextual and broadcast advertising [S2].

Internet services that are funded by advertising could lose revenue, and some of that loss could show up as more paywalls or subscriptions for users — the bill includes no study or transition plan for this [S2].
The per-violation private damages and the invalidation of arbitration agreements could invite high-volume lawsuits that fall hardest on smaller firms [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: strong privacy protection for hundreds of millions of internet users versus the end of a targeting model that funds much of the free internet and is a cheap marketing tool for small firms. The bill leans hard toward privacy — its contextual-ad and geographic-targeting carve-outs soften the blow for local commerce, but it offers no transition support for the ad-funded web. It was introduced, never debated, so its design was never tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee in September 2023, and it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Banning Surveillance Advertising Act on September 18, 2023, joined by Rep. Jan Schakowsky [S1][S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and four days later to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
Only one additional member cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor ever signed on [S3].
No further action was taken: the action history ends at the subcommittee referral, meaning no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote ever occurred [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ad-tech companies, social media platforms, and data brokers kept the targeted-advertising business model and its revenue untouched, and advertisers kept buying precise audience targeting. Internet users kept the same privacy status quo.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, and both the sponsor and all cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican joined, so any floor fate was never tested.

industries.industry: Digital advertising platforms and ad-tech intermediaries
industries.note: Their core model — collecting personal data to decide which individual sees which ad — would be illegal. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the privacy of the people using their services.
Supplying lists, contact information, and device identifiers for ad targeting would be barred, cutting off a major line of business built on personal data.
Advertisers would lose the ability to reach specific customers cheaply and precisely, but small advertisers would no longer compete against rivals with vastly larger data operations.
